summary: Consolidates updates to IETF administrative terminology after the 2018 move to IASA 2.0, which changed several position titles and organizational relationships referenced in other documents. Rather than reissue each document, this gives the updates in one place.

plainLanguage.summary: When job titles change, it is easier to publish one list of the new names than to rewrite every old paper.

questions: why did ietf reorganize its administration
what changed in ietf job titles
subtitle: How IASA 2.0 reorganized IETF's administrative structure and what changed in the terminology

tldr.problem: In 2018, the IETF reorganized its administrative support structure (IASA 2.0), which changed several position titles and organizational relationships referenced in seven existing documents.
tldr.mechanism: Rather than updating each of the seven affected documents individually, this RFC consolidates all the terminology changes in one place, specifying which positions were renamed and how.
tldr.outcome: The IETF Executive Director position was split into two roles: the Managing Director of the IETF Secretariat (taking most of the old responsibilities) and a new Executive Director for the IETF Administration LLC.

today: RFC 8717 is a Best Current Practice document that consolidates the administrative terminology changes from IASA 2.0. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the authoritative guide to how IASA 2.0 changed position titles and organizational references in IETF governance documents.

sections.title: Why This Document Exists
sections.content:
In 2018, the IETF moved to a new administrative structure called IASA 2.0. Rather than just changing how things worked internally, this restructuring also changed several job titles and reporting relationships that were mentioned in other IETF documents. Instead of reissuing seven separate RFC documents to fix those references, this RFC consolidates all the changes in one place.

The documents being updated are about how the IETF runs: the organizations involved, working group procedures, the IESG charter, decision-making processes, and other governance matters.
sections.plainLanguage: When a company reorganizes and job titles change, it is easier to send one memo saying "here are the new names" than to rewrite every policy handbook.

sections.title: The Main Change: From One Director to Two
sections.content:
The most significant change is how the IETF Executive Director position was split. Under IASA 2.0, the IETF Executive Director was split into two separate roles:

Managing Director, IETF Secretariat: This person takes on most of the day-to-day responsibilities that the old Executive Director had. They run the IETF Secretariat and handle the administrative support activities.

Executive Director (for the IETF Administration LLC): This is a new officer position within the IETF Administration LLC (LLC), which is a separate legal entity that handles IETF business matters.

This change applies to seven RFCs: 2028, 2418, 3710, 3929, 4633, and 6702. Each of these documents is updated to use the new terminology where appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: The old "Executive Director" job was split into two: a Managing Director who runs the office, and an Executive Director for the LLC legal entity.

sections.title: Which Documents Are Affected
sections.content:
This RFC updates terminology in the following documents:

  • RFC 2028: The Organizations Involved in the IETF Standards Process
  • RFC 2418: IETF Working Group Guidelines and Procedures
  • RFC 3710: An IESG Charter
  • RFC 3929: Alternative Decision Making Processes for Consensus-Blocked Decisions in the IETF
  • RFC 4633: Experiment in Long-Term Suspensions From Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) Mailing Lists
  • RFC 6702: Promoting Compliance with Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) Disclosure Rules

For all these documents, the changes are straightforward: wherever the IETF Executive Director is mentioned, it is replaced with Managing Director, IETF Secretariat (except in cases noted below).
sections.plainLanguage: Six old documents talk about the Executive Director role, so they all get updated with the new job title.

sections.title: Removing the Role Where It No Longer Applies
sections.content:
In some cases, the IETF Executive Director role (whether old or new) is no longer appropriate for the function described. For instance, RFC 3005 (IETF Discussion List Charter) used to authorize the IETF Executive Director to restrict who could post to the IETF discussion list. Under IASA 2.0, this responsibility no longer belongs to either variant of that position, so the authorization is simply removed rather than reassigned.

In these cases, the reference to the position is dropped entirely, not replaced with the new title.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old rules let the Executive Director do things that are not their job anymore, so those rules just get deleted instead of updated.

sections.title: Documents That Are Now Historic
sections.content:
The RFC also requests that RFC 3716 (The IETF in the Large: Administration and Execution) be marked as Historic. RFC 3716 was a report from an IAB committee that guided the original IASA structure. Since IASA 2.0 replaces that original structure, RFC 3716 is no longer current.

Two other RFCs that had already been obsoleted by RFC 8179 are also mentioned: RFC 3979 and RFC 4879. These dealt with intellectual property procedures and have already been superseded.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old documents about how the IETF used to run are marked as no longer current, since the organization has moved on.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: This RFC is purely about terminology and organizational structure. It makes no changes to how IETF protocols work or how Internet security is handled. The changes are administrative only and have no effect on Internet security.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing job titles does not make the Internet more or less secure.
